title: run, ps, logs, exec
summary: The everyday commands for starting, inspecting, entering and cleaning up containers.

steps.title: The daily toolkit
body: ```text
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27     create + start, in the background (-d)
docker ps                               list RUNNING containers
docker ps -a                            list ALL containers, including exited ones
docker logs web                         what PID 1 wrote to stdout/stderr
docker logs -f --tail 50 web            follow the log, starting 50 lines back
docker exec -it web sh                  start an extra shell INSIDE the running container
docker stop web                         graceful stop (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 s)
docker rm web                           delete the stopped container
docker rm -f web                        stop and delete in one go
`docker ps` prints a table:
```text
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE        COMMAND                  CREATED         STATUS          PORTS                  NAMES
3f2a9c1d0b7e   nginx:1.27   "/docker-entrypoint.…"   2 minutes ago   Up 2 minutes    0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp   web
The `STATUS` column is the first thing to read when something is wrong: `Up 2 minutes`, `Exited (1) 5 seconds ago`, `Restarting (1) 3 seconds ago`, `Up 1 hour (unhealthy)`.

steps.prompt: Match each command to its effect.
pairs: lists every container, including exited ones
streams the main process's output as it is written
opens a shell inside the running container

steps.prompt: You run these three commands. What does the last one print? (One line per container, newest first.)
steps.explain: `docker ps` only shows running containers. `migrate` exited as soon as its command finished, so you would need `docker ps -a` to see it.
With `-a` exited containers appear too. `docker ps` lists newest first, and `migrate` was created after `web`.

steps.title: logs and exec
body: **`docker logs`** does not read files inside the container. It shows what the **main process** wrote to **stdout and stderr**, which Docker captures. If your app writes only to `/var/log/app.log`, `docker logs` stays empty.
**`docker exec`** starts an **extra** process in a container that is **already running**, sharing its filesystem and network:
```text
docker exec web cat /etc/nginx/nginx.conf     run one command
docker exec -it web sh                        interactive shell (-i keep stdin open, -t allocate a terminal)

Many slim images have `sh` but not `bash`, and distroless images have no shell at all. `exec` into a **stopped** container is impossible: there is nothing running to join. For that, read its logs, or start a new container from the same image with a different command (you will do that in the production module).

steps.prompt: The `api` container crashed and shows `Exited (1)`. You run `docker exec -it api sh`. What happens?
options: An error: the container is not running, so there is no process to join
A shell opens inside the stopped container
Docker restarts the container and opens a shell
A shell opens in a fresh container from the same image
steps.explain: `exec` needs a running container. Start with `docker logs api` to see why it exited.

steps.prompt: Open an interactive shell inside the running container `web` (built from an Alpine image).
steps.explain: `exec` joins a running container, `-it` gives you an interactive terminal, and Alpine ships `sh` rather than `bash`.

steps.prompt: Arrange a typical check-and-clean-up session for a container you started in the background.
steps.explain: You can look at `ps` and `logs` in either order, but both need the container to exist, and `rm` needs it stopped.

steps.title: Find the crashed container
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal, with a small shop on it: `api`, `worker`, `cache` and a finished `report`.
Someone says "the shop is broken". Investigate, without removing or restarting anything:
1. One container stopped with an error. Write its name and exit code into `~/answers/crashed.txt`, like `job 0`.
2. Write the error line it printed into `~/answers/cause.txt`.
3. The API reads `/etc/shop/api.conf` **inside its container**. Write its `max_connections` value into `~/answers/max.txt`.

checks.name: crashed.txt names the crashed container and its exit code
checks.fail: Not quite. Write `NAME CODE` (for example `job 0`) for the container that stopped with an error. `docker ps -a` shows it.

checks.name: cause.txt has the error line from its log
checks.cmd: grep -qF 'cannot connect to queue at rabbit:5672' ~/answers/cause.txt
checks.fail: `cause.txt` should hold the error line the crashed container wrote. `docker logs NAME` shows stdout and stderr.

checks.name: max.txt has the API's max_connections setting
checks.fail: `max.txt` should hold the number from `max_connections=` in `/etc/shop/api.conf` inside the running `api` container. `docker exec api cat ...`.

checks.name: the containers are still there to investigate
checks.cmd: docker container inspect api worker cache report >/dev/null 2>&1 && test "$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Running}}' api)" = true
checks.fail: Some containers were removed or `api` was stopped. Press Reset scenario: investigating should not destroy the evidence.

hints: `docker ps` lists running containers only; `docker ps -a` shows the exited ones with `Exited (CODE)`.
`docker logs worker` shows what its main process wrote to stdout and stderr, even after it stopped.
`docker exec api cat /etc/shop/api.conf` runs one command inside the running container.
steps.explain: `ps -a` found the exit code, `logs` read the stderr of a container that is no longer running, and `exec` looked inside one that is. Those three commands answer most "my container is broken" tickets, and none of them changes anything, so the evidence survives for the next person.
